header: IN THE PESHAWAR HIGH COURT, MINGORA BENCH
Syed Muhammad Ikran and another v. Mst. Gulshan Bibi and others
For Appellants Mr. Ashfaq Ahmad, Advocate
For Respondents Mr. Arif Ullah, Advocate
Assistance Mr. Qaiser Abbas, Civil Judge/Former Research
body: *** Dr. Khurshid Iqbal, J.- 1. This regular first appeal against order, instituted on 25.08.2025 under section 8 of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Enforcement of Women’s Property Rights Act, 2019 (Act No. XLIV of 2019) (hereinafter ‘the Act’), calls in question the final order dated 12.08.2025 passed by the learned Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Ombudsperson. Respondents Nos. 1 to 3, who are stated to be sisters of the appellants, approached the Ombudsperson claiming their lawful shares in the estate of their deceased father, Mian Abdullah. Respondent No. 4 is described as another brother of the parties. The appeal raises the limits of summary adjudication under the Act where the identity and ownership of the subject property depend upon disputed transactions alleged to have taken place during the lifetime of the predecessor.

2. The complaint was received by the learned Ombudsperson on 8 August 2023. The complainants asserted that late Mian Abdullah owned land measuring 34 kanals and 7 marlas at Ganderoshah, Tehsil Dargai, District Malakand; that they were entitled to their respective shares under Muslim law of inheritance; and that the appellants had, through force and coercion, excluded them from possession and enjoyment of the property and its usufruct. These allegations were disputed. The relationship among the parties was not, however, denied.

3. On 11.08.2023, the Registrar of the Ombudsperson’s office addressed the Deputy Commissioner, Malakand, requesting a comprehensive inquiry and report. Copies were also endorsed to Syed Muhammad Ikram and others. A Girdawar of Circle Dargai reported on 21.09.2023 that formal land records were not maintained in Malakand and transfers were commonly effected through stamp-paper instruments. That report was forwarded to the Deputy Commissioner. Its observation concerning the mode of recording transactions did not, by itself, establish ownership of the disputed land in either side. Page 2 of 14 4. An application seeking appointment of a local commission was presented on 02.01.2024. The copy reproduced in the record does not identify its maker by name or signature. The endorsement of the learned Ombudsperson consists of the word ‘Allowed’ followed by a signature, without recorded reasons. Although the absence of elaborate reasons at this preliminary stage may not, standing alone, determine the legality of the entire proceedings, the scope and evidentiary purpose of the commission must be considered in light of the procedure prescribed by the Act.

5. The appellants submitted their written statement on 13.02.2024, raising objections of limitation, want of cause of action, jurisdiction, estoppel, mala fides and non-joinder, besides disputing the factual foundation of the complaint. Their central case was that substantial portions of the property claimed by the complainants had ceased to belong to Mian Abdullah during his lifetime or had never formed part of his estate. They relied upon a deed dated 18.03.1992 as evidencing a gift by the father in favour of his sons, and a deed dated 07.04.1985 as evidencing the independent purchase of land at Nashoro Kandao from Ghulam Said. They also referred to a further sale transaction dated 20.09.2009, concerning part of the property.

6. The precise property said to be covered by these instruments is itself material. The appellants’ version, as subsequently explained by learned counsel, is that the deed of gift dated 18 March 1992 relates to residential accommodation comprising a house of 20 marlas for appellants Ikram and Iftikhar and a house of 9 marlas for appellant Farooq; that Farooq purchased land measuring approximately 48 kanals at Nashoro Kandao under the instrument of 7 April 1985; and that the instrument of 20 September 2009 records a subsequent transfer to co-appellants Ikram and Iftikhar. The description of the 2009 transaction in the written-statement summary is not entirely consistent with that submission, while the land area mentioned at different stages also varies. The significance is not that either account must now be accepted, but that the identity of the property and the chain of claimed title require determination upon the actual instruments and admissible evidence.

7. The local commission consisted of two advocates. It reported having inspected the site on 14.02.2024 in the presence of the parties and having recorded their statements. Its report, submitted on 06.03.2024, did not confine itself to identifying the land or recording physical features. It pronounced upon the legal efficacy of the 1992 gift, observing that, even if genuine, the gift was intended to deprive female heirs of their shares and therefore had no legal effect. It further concluded that land measuring 30 kanals and 12 marlas at Nashoro Kandao belonged to the deceased and that the complainants were entitled to inherit therefrom.

8. In rejecting the asserted purchase of the Nashoro Kandao land, the commission recorded that the appellants had produced an unattested handwritten stamp-paper instrument, had neither identified the land to the commission nor Page 3 of 14 produced a witness to the transaction, and had not established a source of income at the date of purchase. These observations are relevant to questions requiring proof; they do not dispense with the need to determine the admissibility, authenticity and legal effect of the instrument in proceedings competent to resolve disputed title. Nor could the absence of evidence before a local commission conclusively establish an adverse title where the transaction itself required a proper trial.

9. By the impugned final order of 12 August 2025, the learned Ombudsperson adopted the conclusions of the commission and directed the Deputy Commissioner, Malakand, to ensure delivery of possession in accordance with its report within 15 days. The persons in occupation were directed to hand over possession. The District Police Officer was also required to maintain law and order and provide protection in implementing the direction.

10. The appeal was filed on 25.08.2025, within the forty-five-day period prescribed by section 8 of the Act. On 02.09.2025 it was admitted for regular hearing and an order of status quo was made. Respondents thereafter filed Civil Miscellaneous Application No. 2520 of 2025, annexing what was described as a copy of a Patwari’s report concerning delivery of possession on 29.08.2025. On 03.10.2025, this Court suspended the operation of the impugned order and restrained further consequential proceedings in the manner recorded in its interim order. The actual extent and legal effect of any possession delivered on 29.08.2025 remain disputed and cannot be inferred conclusively from the production of that report alone.

11. Mr Khalid Khan, learned counsel for the appellants, argued that the learned Ombudsperson had treated an intricate dispute of title as if it were a simple case of withholding an admitted inheritance. He relied upon the gift deed dated 18.03.1992 and upon the assertion that declaration, acceptance and delivery of possession were recorded therein. As to the land at Nashoro Kandao, he referred to the purchase deed dated 07.04.1985 and the subsequent deed dated 20.09.2009, submitting that the latter specifically recited the former transaction. These documents, he contended, made it necessary to assess the appropriate statutory route under sections 4 and 6, rather than to accept a local commission’s legal opinion. He also challenged the adequacy of hearing and requested that the appeal be allowed notwithstanding the disputed execution report.

12. Mr. Arifullah, learned counsel for the complainants, supported the impugned order. He submitted that the gift and sale instruments were neither established nor shown to concern the property in question, and described them as unregistered and manipulated. According to him, the appellants were heard by the commission, their defence was noticed in the final order and the deprivation of the sisters’ inheritance justified relief under the Act. He further relied upon the asserted delivery of possession to contend that the appeal had lost its efficacy. The broad submission concerning the prevalence of exclusion of female heirs was pressed as supporting the statutory purpose; it remains Page 4 of 14 necessary, however, to decide the particular dispute upon its own facts and the limits of the statutory jurisdiction.

13. The submissions and the available record have been considered. The questions arising are whether the complaint, in the face of the rival instruments and competing claims of ownership, could lawfully be determined by summary directions under sections 4 and 5; whether the process followed afforded the statutory opportunity to meet the material relied upon; and whether the claimed implementation of the order affected the competence or relief available in this appeal. These questions do not require this Court to determine finally the validity of the gift or sale deeds, or the respective inheritance shares.

14. Section 8 expressly permits an aggrieved person to appeal to this Court within forty-five days of an order of the Ombudsperson. The present challenge to the final order, filed thirteen days after its date, is therefore within time. The fact that steps may subsequently have been taken in execution does not extinguish the statutory right of appeal. Otherwise, the efficacy of section 8 would depend upon the speed with which an impugned order could be enforced, a construction not supported by the statutory text. Section 12, which bars interference by other courts and authorities in proceedings under the Act, must be read harmoniously with the express appellate jurisdiction conferred by section 8; it cannot nullify that jurisdiction.
15. The statutory purpose is stated in the preamble of the Act in the following terms:

WHEREAS, it is expedient to provide for the protection of the rights of ownership and possession of properties owned by women, ensuring that such rights are not violated by means of harassment, coercion, force or fraud and for the matters connected therewith or incidental thereto [.] 16. The statutory purpose deserves more than a formal acknowledgment. The exclusion of daughters and sisters from property which devolves upon them by law is not a private family courtesy withheld, but a denial of a legal right. Inheritance rights do not depend upon the goodwill or permission of male relations. The law must be alert to the social conditions in which women are pressured into silence, made to acquiesce in transactions they do not understand, or kept from the enjoyment of their shares. Articles 23, 24 and 25 of the Constitution, read within the constitutional commitment to the protection of the family under Article 35, reinforce the importance of effective remedies. Yet that commitment is vindicated, not weakened, by adjudication according to law: a protective statute cannot be interpreted so as to deprive a party of the process which the statute itself commands.

17. A familiar distinction in the common law is between the existence of a right and the procedure by which its infringement may lawfully be redressed. The maxim ubi jus ibi remedium expresses the obligation of the legal system to provide a remedy for an established right; it does not dispense with the adjudication required to establish the right where it is genuinely disputed. Page 5 of 14 Equally, audi alteram partem is not an obstacle to substantive justice but a condition of it. Legislative solicitude for vulnerable claimants calls for urgency, care and effective relief. It does not authorise an executive functionary to decide title on impressions, or a court to disregard the legislature’s chosen division between summary restoration and civil trial.

18. The enactment is remedial, but remedial legislation is not legislation without boundaries. A court interpreting it must be attentive both to the mischief addressed and to the means lawfully prescribed for its correction. In Mirza Shaukat , the Hon’ble Supreme Court emphasised that legislative intention is gathered primarily from the words enacted, and that a preamble cannot displace an unambiguous substantive provision. A five-member Bench of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Ghulam Haider , likewise underscored that a legislative object must be achieved through the method selected by the legislature; and in D.G. Khan Cement, the Court explained the need for harmonious construction across the statute. The concluding words of this preamble concerning incidental matters cannot accordingly create a plenary jurisdiction over contested civil title.

19. The distinction between a liberal construction of remedial provisions and an impermissible enlargement of jurisdiction also finds support in Abdul Aziz . That decision recognizes that relief-giving provisions may warrant a generous construction consistent with their terms. Here, the remedial purpose therefore favours prompt preliminary action, preservation of property and expeditious referral; it does not justify reading the express duty to make a reference under section 6 out of the Act.

20. The procedure under section 4 is deliberately graduated. Sub-section (2) requires a preliminary assessment and, where further probe is necessary, contemplates a reference to the concerned Deputy Commissioner, who must notify the complainant and her adversaries and submit a summary inquiry report. Under sub-section (3), orders under section 5 may be passed where the matter does not require detailed investigation or recording of evidence. Sub-section (4) permits further summary enquiry, while sub-section (5) requires that the Deputy Commissioner’s report and the conclusions of the Ombudsperson’s own enquiry be confronted to the parties and objections invited before the final decision. Section 5(1) authorises a restorative direction only upon a finding, reached on conclusion of proceedings under section 4, that the complainant has been illegally deprived of ownership or possession of her property.

21. Section 6(1), entitled ‘Reference to the Court’, operates notwithstanding sections 4 and 5. It requires the Ombudsperson, whenever the preliminary Mirza Shaukat Baig and others v. Shahid Jamil and others (PLD 2005 SC 530, paragraph 13), drawing upon Shahid Nabi Malik v. Chief Election Commissioner (PLD 1997 SC 32). Ghulam Haider and others v. Murad through legal representatives and others (PLD 2012 SC 501).
D.G. Khan Cement Company Ltd. and others v. Federation of Pakistan and others (2004 SCMR 456, paragraph 18).

Abdul Aziz Zehri v. Chairman, Selection Committee (1992 SCMR 1078). Page 6 of 14 assessment, the Deputy Commissioner’s report or a subsequent summary inquiry discloses a need for ‘in-depth enquiry, investigation or detailed recording of evidence or intricate adjudication’, to formulate a reference together with the collected material and send it to the competent Civil Court. The prescribed period of sixty days is expressed as preferential; it does not enlarge the Ombudsperson’s adjudicative competence merely because that period has elapsed.

22. Sub-section (2) of section 6 directs the competent Civil Court to entertain that reference as a civil suit and proceed under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and the relevant rules. The opening non obstante words of section 6(1), its express enumeration of the circumstances requiring a reference, and the mandatory expression ‘shall’ make the legislative division of functions clear. The Ombudsperson is not powerless merely because an adversary denies title; equally, the Ombudsperson cannot retain an intricate controversy for final adjudication merely by describing the disputed evidence as unsatisfactory. The relevant threshold is whether a genuine and material issue, necessary to the grant of relief, requires the evidentiary and adjudicative processes of a Civil Court. A bare or contrived denial does not suffice; a substantial contest over the source, identity or transfer of title, supported by particulars requiring proof, does.

23. In Falak Shehnaz , this Court considered the constitutional and procedural limits of measures affecting disputed property under the Act, particularly where joint rights and existing civil proceedings were involved. The judgment distinguished protective measures from orders depriving persons in possession of the actual use of property without the requisite legal basis and identified the statutory difficulty in delivering exclusive physical possession from undivided joint property. Its material relevance here is the insistence that the protection of female ownership cannot dispense with the legal mechanism by which contested title or separate possession must first be established.

24. A closely related application of section 6 appears in Inayatullah In that matter, this Court held that disputes over inheritance, partition and entitlement to possession, involving rival civil claims and requiring evidence from both sides, could not be finally resolved through the Ombudsperson’s summary procedure. The case was remitted for action in accordance with law. That conclusion accords with the present Act’s division of responsibility between an accessible administrative remedy and adjudication before an independent Civil Court.

25. The same question received direct consideration in Ali Asghar decided by this Court on 31.10.2025 in a consolidated group of appeals, and by Honourable Mst. Falak Shehnaz and another v. Mst. Farah Deeba and others (PLD 2025 Peshawar 1). Inayatullah and others v. Mst. Safra Begum (2024 CLC1793).
Ali Asghar v. Mst. Farkhanda Rani and another (2026 CLC 1159).

Page 7 of 14 Supreme Court in Naheed Shah Afridi decided on 29.10.2026. The Court distinguished cases involving persons with no arguable title from disputes between co-owners, and held that the Ombudsperson could not award exclusive physical possession of an undivided inherited share without lawful partition, nor conclusively determine intricate title disputes reserved by section 6 for the Civil Court. The precise status of the present holdings is disputed, but that is itself the reason to examine the documents and the character of possession before ordering physical delivery. The principles operate to preserve, not extinguish, a woman’s undivided proprietary share.

26. The substantive right of women to inherit must be understood with equal clarity. In Falak Shehnaz this Court distinguished lawful protective measures from coercive interference with use and possession, in a dispute over inherited joint property. In Ghulam Qasim the Hon’ble Supreme Court addressed the wrongful exclusion of female heirs. More recently, the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Abrar Hussain , emphasized that succession vests immediately in the lawful heirs upon death and scrutinized an alleged lifetime gift in favour of one son which had not been established by reliable evidence. These decisions do not declare every genuine lifetime gift benefiting a son invalid. They establish that a gift relied upon to defeat an otherwise lawful inheritance claim must be proved by its beneficiary through the requirements of the governing law.

27. In Noor Muhammad , the Hon’ble Supreme Court examined an alleged oral gift by female heirs to male relatives after the inheritance had already vested in those women. The Court required proof of the essential elements of gift and warned that a mutation, by itself, does not constitute title. The distinction in chronology is important: this case concerns an alleged disposition by Mian Abdullah during his own lifetime. It remains necessary to ask whether he in fact owned and validly transferred the identified property; the courts should not confuse an alleged donor’s lifetime power of disposition with an heir’s later purported surrender of an inheritance already acquired.

28. The Hon’ble Federal Constitutional Court in Bibi Amina required heightened scrutiny of compromises, gifts, mutations and other transactions which purportedly extinguish or compromise women’s vested inheritance rights. The judgment arose from a disputed compromise affecting the shares of female legal heirs. Its central insistence upon genuine consent, proof and judicial vigilance is relevant by analogy, but its factual and legal setting is not identical to a father’s purported gift made before death. In this appeal that distinction Mst. Naheed Shah Afridi and another v. Muzaffar Shah Afridi and another (C.P.L.A. Nos. 2630 and 2639 of 2026, decided on 29.10.2026).
Falak Shehnaz, supra n. 5.

Ghulam Qasim and others v. Mst Razia Begum and others (PLD 2021 SC 812). Abrar Hussain v. Mst. Bibi Shahida and others (PLD 2026 SC 42). Noor Mohammad and others v. Ghulam Haider and others (2026 SCP 211). Mst. Bibi Amina and others v. Shamsullah and others (CPLA No. 143-Q of 2025, decided on 4 June 2026).
Page 8 of 14 reinforces the need for an evidentiary trial rather than supplying a shortcut to invalidate or uphold the 1992 instrument.

29. The local commission’s treatment of the gift dated 18.03.1992 illustrates the distinction. It reasoned that the gift, even if genuine, could not have legal effect because its purpose was to exclude female heirs from future inheritance. Such reasoning proceeds from the result of the disposition to its invalidity without determining the essential factual and legal questions: the donor’s title and capacity; the actual property gifted; declaration of gift; acceptance by the donees; delivery or legally recognised transfer of possession; and any pleaded ground of sham transaction, fraud, undue influence or want of free consent. The timing of a disposition during the owner’s lifetime is also materially different from a purported relinquishment of an inheritance already devolved. None of these issues could properly be disposed of by treating a prediction of future disadvantage, without more, as a conclusive legal test.

30. The evidentiary burden in the competent forum will therefore require a precise and discriminating approach. The persons claiming through the gift must establish the donor’s title, a genuine declaration, acceptance and delivery of possession as required by Muslim law, whether actual or legally sufficient constructive delivery on the established facts. The women remain entitled to challenge authenticity, capacity, the property description, the alleged change of dominion and any asserted mala fides. The ultimate finding must depend on proof, not upon the bare fact that male donees may benefit from a valid disposition. The principles concerning a gift and a deceased owner’s continuing possession are also explained in Abrar Hussain and in Ghulam Ali.

31. The rival sale documents require a similar inquiry. The instrument of 07.04.1985 is said to establish an independent purchase from Ghulam Said; the 20.09.2009 instrument is said to trace title to that earlier transaction. Their genuineness, execution, identification of the land, relationship to the property claimed as inheritance, applicable formal requirements and the parties’ possession are disputed. Questions concerning attestation, registration and the evidentiary sufficiency of an instrument cannot be decided in abstraction from its nature, the law governing the transaction and the proof adduced. The commission’s doubts concerning an alleged purchaser’s earning capacity may form part of an evidentiary evaluation; they cannot, by themselves, create ownership in another person.

32. A further difficulty concerns identification of the very subject matter of the order. The complaint refers to 34 kanals and 7 marlas at Ganderoshah; the commission’s conclusion refers to 30 kanals and 12 marlas at Nashoro Kandao; the asserted purchase has been described as relating to about 48 kanals; and the later transaction has also been described by reference to 32 kanals. The record Abrar Hussain, supra n.10. Ghulam Ali and others v. Mst. Ghulam Sarwar Naqvi (PLD 1990 SC 1).

Page 9 of 14 recounted before this Court does not provide an accepted plan or other common description establishing whether these are wholly or partly the same parcels, adjoining holdings or distinct properties. This distinction is fundamental. A direction to deliver possession must identify, with sufficient precision, the land to which it relates and the person whose legally established right entitles him or her to receive it. An executive officer cannot be left to resolve those disputed matters of title by interpreting an uncertain operative direction.

33. The Girdawar’s observation that formal revenue records were not maintained in the locality reinforces, rather than removes, the need for careful proof of title and identification. In a locality where private instruments, possession and surrounding circumstances may assume greater evidentiary significance, the absence of conventional entries does not entitle an adjudicator to prefer one claim without testing the competing material. Equally, the absence of such entries does not extinguish the complainants’ lawful inheritance, if the property is ultimately shown to have belonged to the deceased at his death.

34. The powers and duties of a local commission must also be kept distinct from those of the adjudicating authority. Inspection of the site, measurement, identification of physical features and recording of observations may aid an inquiry, subject to lawful appointment and procedural safeguards. A commission comprising advocates does not thereby acquire jurisdiction to invalidate a gift, pronounce upon the credibility of an alleged purchase as a final issue, or determine the shares of heirs in disputed property. Its report is material to be assessed; it is not a substitute for the statutory inquiry by the Deputy Commissioner where section 4(2) is engaged, nor for a reasoned judicial determination when section 6 applies.

35. The appellants’ presence before the commission and the opportunity said to have been afforded to make statements at the site do not answer the objection of fair hearing in its entirety. Section 4(5) contemplates confrontation with the relevant inquiry findings, an opportunity to submit objections, and an independent decision by the Ombudsperson. The materials summarized here do not demonstrate whether the commission’s adverse conclusions were separately supplied to the appellants and considered upon reasoned objections before they were adopted. In any event, the decisive defect is not merely one of hearing: it is the use of a summary process to render conclusive findings on transactions and property identification which required detailed adjudication under section

6. 36. Nor was the omission of a reasoned order appointing the commission immaterial to the subsequent inquiry. The one-word endorsement on an unsigned application does not disclose the question referred to the commission, the limits of the mandate or why that mode of inquiry was appropriate. These circumstances call for caution before treating the report as the foundation for coercive delivery of possession. They do not require a declaration that every Page 10 of 14 observation of the commission is devoid of evidentiary value; a competent court may assess any relevant, duly proved material in accordance with law.

37. The learned Ombudsperson was therefore required to distinguish between the preliminary question whether the complainants disclosed a plausible deprivation of property rights and the much further question whether the particular properties were legally part of the deceased’s estate and capable of delivery to them in severalty. The first could plainly be investigated under the Act. The latter could not, on the present record, be conclusively answered without deciding the claimed lifetime gift, the contested purchases, the extent of the holdings and, where appropriate, the lawful partition of any undivided estate. The Act itself provides the answer to that jurisdictional difficulty in section 6.

38. This conclusion does not turn on any presumption that the complainants have fabricated their grievance. A sister’s inheritance claim is not weakened because it is resisted, and a male heir’s prolonged possession does not, without more, prove an extinguishment of the co-heirs’ shares. Where the predecessor’s ownership of a particular parcel is established, its devolution is governed by succession and the requirements of partition or appropriate joint possession. Where the predecessor’s ownership is itself seriously disputed, that anterior fact must first be lawfully determined. These are complementary propositions, not competing policies.

39. The objection that the complainants are sisters who have been excluded by their brothers deserves serious consideration; the law recognizes neither a custom defeating a female heir’s prescribed share nor a presumption that possession by male relatives amounts to exclusive ownership. But it is equally inconsistent with due process to assume that the existence of a family relationship establishes the deceased’s ownership of every disputed parcel. The claim of inheritance is derivative of the property vested in the deceased at death. The extent of that estate is a matter to be proved, particularly where a specified portion is claimed under transactions said to predate death.

40. On these facts, the disputes are neither peripheral nor manufactured by a merely general denial. They concern identified instruments bearing dates, purported parties and claimed property descriptions, together with contradictory assertions about physical possession and title. They bear directly upon whether the statutory precondition to a restorative order under section 5(1) is satisfied. The report itself addressed these questions by purporting to determine their legal merits. That course confirms the need for detailed recording of evidence and intricate adjudication, rather than providing a lawful substitute for them.

41. The impugned order cannot be sustained merely because it reproduces or notices the appellants’ defence. A reasoned determination must engage with a material defence according to the powers and procedure of the forum. Where the statutory scheme requires reference of a class of disputes to the Civil Court, the Ombudsperson cannot satisfy that requirement by rejecting the defence upon Page 11 of 14 a commission’s opinion and proceeding directly to the coercive remedy under section 5. To that extent, the order exceeds the proper scope of the summary jurisdiction and suffers from a material error of law.

42. The contention that possession was delivered on 29.08.2025 does not render the appeal infructuous. The appeal had already been instituted on 25 August 2025. Although the reported delivery preceded the status quo order of 02.09.2025, implementation of an appealable order is subject to the legal consequences of its eventual appellate determination. What the Patwari’s report establishes, the precise land allegedly delivered, the persons to whom delivery was effected and the actual state of possession cannot be finally determined on the present description of a copy filed with a miscellaneous application. Those matters must be addressed upon proper evidence by the competent forum; neither the alleged execution nor its subsequent suspension decides title.

43. The legal consequence of setting aside an order already carried into execution is a separate question from the merits of the original claim. A right of appeal would be substantially impaired if the authority whose order is challenged could make the appeal practically ineffectual merely by executing it before an appellate hearing. That is why the common law recognizes restitution as a consequence of reversal: a party should not retain a procedural advantage obtained solely through an order which has subsequently been set aside. This principle is reflected in section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. It is not suggested that section 144, which speaks directly to a decree reversed or varied by a Court, applies in every particular to an order of the Ombudsperson; the principle of restoring the position disturbed by a reversed order nevertheless informs the consequential powers necessary to give effect to this Court’s appellate decision under section 8.

44. In The Land Acquisition Collector , this Court explained the restorative principle embodied in section 144, namely that, to the practicable extent, the benefit taken under a decree later reversed must be returned. The present case requires a carefully confined application: if the Deputy Commissioner or another state functionary actually delivered specified property to respondents Nos. 1 to 3 on 29 August 2025 exclusively pursuant to the order dated 12 August 2025, the execution has lost its legal foundation. Such possession must, subject to reliable identification of the parcels and the persons displaced, be restored to the position immediately before that execution. It would not be just to permit the coercive operation of an unlawful order to create a factual advantage while the rightful title is awaiting adjudication.

45. The restoration now contemplated is therefore restitutionary and not proprietary. It neither confirms the appellants’ asserted title nor excludes the sisters’ share in property which may be established as their father’s estate. Equally, it does not authorize displacement of an independent possessor, The Land Acquisition Collector (WAPDA) v. Jehanzeb Khan and others (RFA No. 127-A of 2010, decided on 14 November 2019).

Page 12 of 14 undoing an unrelated transaction, or disturbing any possession that was not actually changed by execution of the impugned order. Inasmuch as the reported delivery occurred before the interim status quo order of 02.09.2025, the case is not treated as one of breach of that later order. The duty to reverse the execution follows from the appellate decision setting aside its legal source.

46. For these reasons, the question framed above is answered in the negative. The complaint plainly invoked a protective purpose of the Act, and the sisters’ claims warrant serious and timely adjudication. Nevertheless, the rival claims to title, the alleged completed gift, the contested purchases, conflicting property descriptions and the possible requirement of lawful partition made detailed recording of evidence and intricate adjudication necessary. The learned Ombudsperson ought, under the mandatory terms of section 6(1), to have formulated a reference to the competent Civil Court instead of finally deciding these disputes upon the commission’s report. Nothing in this conclusion finds the gift or sale deeds genuine, or the complainants’ inheritance claims false.

47. The appeal is accordingly allowed and the final order dated 12.08.2025 is set aside, together with its directions for delivery of possession and all consequential acts purportedly founded exclusively upon those directions. The findings of the local commission and Ombudsperson concerning the title, the legal effectiveness of the gift and sale instruments, the extent of the estate, inheritance shares and entitlement to exclusive possession shall not bind the Civil Court. No question of substantive title or partition is finally determined by this judgment.

48. The learned Ombudsperson shall, within thirty days after receipt of a certified copy of this judgment, formulate and transmit a reference under section 6(1) to the Civil Court of competent jurisdiction. The reference shall set out separately the rival property descriptions, the relief sought and the material factual questions requiring determination; it shall be accompanied by the original complaint and reply, the commission’s report, the available inquiry papers, all instruments tendered by the parties, objections, procedural orders and the complete execution and compliance material. Any omission or inconsistency in the property particulars shall be identified rather than resolved by assumption. Under section 6(2), the competent Civil Court shall entertain the reference as a civil suit and proceed in accordance with the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and the relevant rules.

49. The possession, if any, delivered to respondents Nos. 1 to 3 on 29.08.2025 solely in execution of the impugned order shall be reversed, and possession of the precise property so delivered shall be restored to the person or persons from whom it was actually taken immediately before such execution. The purpose is to restore the status quo ante as to execution alone. The reversal shall not amount to a declaration in favour of any alleged owner, a final determination of joint or exclusive possession, or a direction to dispossess any person whose possession was not obtained through that execution.

Page 13 of 14 50. For giving effect to the preceding direction, the Deputy Commissioner, Malakand, shall, within seven days of receiving a certified copy of this judgment, obtain and examine the original contemporaneous record of the alleged delivery of possession dated 29.08.2025, including any possession memorandum, identification of plots or parcels, site plan, names of persons from whom and to whom possession was transferred, witnesses and other contemporaneous material, insofar as these documents actually exist. After notice to the directly affected persons and identification of the property by reference to that record, the Deputy Commissioner shall effect the consequential restoration within twenty-one days of receipt of the judgment, with such lawful police assistance as is necessary to maintain peace, and shall submit an authenticated compliance report to the Registrar of this Court and to the learned Ombudsperson within seven days thereafter.

51. The Deputy Commissioner shall not, in the name of restitution, determine title, partition a joint holding, create a new allotment or enlarge the territorial or physical scope of the delivery evidenced by the contemporaneous record. Where the record does not reliably identify a parcel, the previous actual occupant, or whether possession was in fact transferred in execution of the impugned order, no person shall be removed from that disputed portion on conjecture. The Deputy Commissioner shall promptly place that specific difficulty, with the authentic documents and a reasoned factual report, before the Registrar of this Court for appropriate judicial directions; such an issue shall not impede restoration of any other portion whose execution and previous occupant are ascertainable. No record shall be reconstructed retrospectively and presented as a contemporaneous memorandum.

52. Until the competent Civil Court has considered interim protection, the parties shall not take the law into their own hands, forcibly dispossess another, materially change the character of the disputed land or create a third-party interest by invoking the annulled order. These directions do not prevent an application before the Civil Court for injunction, preservation of property, accounts, appointment of a receiver, or other relief otherwise available in law. On receipt of the reference, the Civil Court shall consider any application for appropriate interim protection expeditiously upon notice and the relevant material, without treating the commission’s findings or the present limited restitutionary direction as an adjudication of title.

53. The Civil Court shall decide all material questions, including whether the properties formed part of the estate at Mian Abdullah’s death, the efficacy of the pleaded lifetime gift and purchase deeds, identification of the parcels, lawful shares, possession, partition and any consequential relief, after allowing the parties a fair opportunity to lead evidence and challenge that of their opponents. Particular vigilance is required where an instrument is said to defeat a woman’s inheritance rights; equally, no presumption of invalidity may take the place of a finding grounded in the governing law and proof. The case should be progressed Page 14 of 14 without avoidable adjournments, having regard to the remedial object of the Act and the passage of time since the complaint was filed.

54. The rights and contentions of the appellants, the complainants and respondent No. 4 are left open on the merits. In particular, nothing herein diminishes the entitlement of respondents Nos. 1 to 3 to their full lawful shares in any property proved to have devolved upon them by inheritance. The restored pre-execution position is provisional and shall abide by such lawful interim and final orders as the competent Civil Court may pass. The appeal stands disposed of in these terms, with no order as to costs.
